title: It's not them, it's us!
author: Dan Winters
summary: Dan Winters, a former elementary principal, reacts to Episode 5 of Sold a Story Season 2 by asking why Direct Instruction and similar explicit teaching are so rarely championed in schools of education and districts. His answer is partly self-critical: proponents have failed to state the end goal of the method. He recalls a respected consultant who claimed Project Follow Through showed DI worked only for discrete skills, when the study also measured problem solving and self esteem and DI performed better on those too. He also recalls a teacher who heard his enthusiasm for DI as a belief that only knowledge accumulation mattered. Winters argues that deep thinkers need a broad knowledge base to draw on, and that novices acquire content differently from how experts discover it. He hopes the series produces dialogue rather than tribal mudslinging, since both camps want critical thinkers and differ only on method.
points: Project Follow Through also measured problem solving and self esteem, and Direct Instruction outperformed on those measures as well as on basic skills.
Advocates of explicit teaching have often failed to say that the end product is critical thinkers and problem solvers, which let critics hear it as knowledge-only.
Deep thinking depends on a broad base of knowledge to analyse and synthesise, so explicit instruction serves the progressive goal of independent thought.
Novices acquire new content differently from how experts discover knowledge, which is the reasoned basis for teaching novices directly.
Winters frames the Sold a Story debate as a shared goal with different methods and hopes for dialogue instead of tribalism.
quotes: I only later realized that Project Follow through also measured problem solving and self esteem, and lo and behold Direct Instruction also performed better on those measures - not just discrete skill and knowledge attainment.

I had failed to articulate a complete theory of learning that resulted in students who were deep thinkers. What my colleague heard was that I believed that all that was important was students accumulating knowledge and not actually thinking for themselves. I had failed to articulate the fact that deep thinkers must have a broad base of knowledge to draw from and only with such information could they form complex thoughts and make unique connections.

In my enthusiasm for sharing the benefits of direct instruction and explicit teaching I failed to articulate the ultimate goal of such practices which is to create critical thinkers and problem solvers who are able to do analysis and synthesis of all that discrete knowledge and skills that they have obtained.
From my experience, one of those reasons that direct instruction has not been embraced is that we proponents have failed to clearly articulate the end product or goal of such instruction.
We want our novice learners to become experts, we just understand that the evidence demonstrates that novice learners acquire new content differently than how experts discover new knowledge.

One way to accomplish that goal is to embrace our similar interests and communicate our common goal that students must become critical thinkers, problem solvers, and demonstrate creativity and innovation. That’s the same goal that progressive educators espouse; we only differ on the methods to achieve that aim.
